generated_for: AWS Certified CloudOps Engineer - Associate (SOA-C03), facts current 2025-2026
how_to_use: Tier S is the cold-recall set: if you cannot recite it without the page, you are not ready. Domain blocks are the sweep. Decision tables are the troubleshooting muscle memory - read the Symptom column first, the Fix column last. Numbers are pure rote; drill them as flashcards.

tier_s_must_memorize_cold.fact:
Default EC2 metrics are hypervisor-visible only: CPU, network, disk I/O of instance-store, status checks. Memory (MemoryUtilization), disk space used, swap, and page file need the CloudWatch agent installed plus an instance profile with CloudWatchAgentServerPolicy.
Basic monitoring = 5-minute periods and is free; detailed monitoring = 1-minute periods and costs extra. Detailed monitoring is NOT 1 second - only custom high-resolution metrics (StorageResolution=1) give 1-second granularity, with high-resolution alarms at 10 s or 30 s.
Alarm has three states: OK, ALARM, INSUFFICIENT_DATA. INSUFFICIENT_DATA is not a failure and does not trigger the ALARM action; if a stopped or terminated instance stops publishing, set Treat missing data as to breaching/notBreaching/ignore/missing deliberately.
M out of N (datapoints to alarm) smooths flapping: alarm fires when M of the last N evaluation periods breach. Composite alarms (ALARM rule over child alarms with AND/OR/NOT) exist to suppress noise, and support an actions-suppressor alarm. A composite alarm can only send an SNS notification, invoke a Lambda function, or raise a Systems Manager OpsItem/incident - it can NEVER perform an EC2 action or an Auto Scaling action, and like any alarm it is capped at 5 actions per alarm state.
Alarm actions: SNS notification, Auto Scaling policy, EC2 action (stop / terminate / reboot / recover), Lambda invoke (a DIRECT alarm action since 2023 - no SNS or EventBridge hop required), Systems Manager OpsItem or incident. EC2 recover only responds to SYSTEM status check failure (StatusCheckFailed_System) - an instance (OS) status failure needs reboot, not recover.
EC2 status checks: system = AWS underlying host/network (fix = stop-start to move host, or recover); instance = OS/network config inside the guest (fix = reboot or repair OS); attached EBS status check = impaired volume.
Metric math and anomaly detection alarms exist; a metric filter on a log group converts log text into a metric so you can alarm on log content (metric filters do not backfill historical logs).

tier_s_must_memorize_cold.topic: Systems Manager suite and managed-node prerequisites
tier_s_must_memorize_cold.fact:
Managed node prerequisites are three and they are the single most tested SSM fact: (1) SSM Agent installed and running, (2) an instance profile role with AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore - or Default Host Management Configuration (DHMC) turned on for the Region, which lets the agent obtain its own credentials so no instance profile is needed, (3) outbound HTTPS 443 network path to ssm, ssmmessages, and ec2messages endpoints - via IGW/NAT or via three interface VPC endpoints.
Session Manager needs NO inbound security group rule, no open port 22, no bastion, no key pair. Session logs go to S3 and/or CloudWatch Logs; KMS can encrypt the session.
Run Command = ad hoc command on many nodes at once, targeted by instance IDs, tags, or a resource group; rate control defaults are MaxConcurrency 50 (a count or a percentage) and MaxErrors 0, so a single failed node stops the whole invocation until you raise MaxErrors.
Automation = multi-step runbook against AWS APIs and instances (AWS-RestartEC2Instance, AWS-StartEC2Instance, AWS-PatchInstanceWithRollback); the standard remediation target for Config rules and EventBridge rules.
State Manager = enforce desired configuration on a schedule (association), e.g. keep agent installed, apply a policy, run Ansible/DSC. Patch Manager = baselines + patch groups (tag key Patch Group) + scan or install, executed inside a Maintenance Window.
Parameter Store: Standard tier free, 4 KB maximum value, 10,000 parameters per account per Region; Advanced tier paid, 8 KB value, 100,000 parameters, plus parameter policies (expiration, notification). SecureString uses KMS. Hierarchies with / allow GetParametersByPath and IAM path-based access.
Fleet Manager = GUI file/registry/user management; Inventory = software and config collection; OpsCenter = aggregated OpsItems; Quick Setup = baseline SSM config across accounts/Regions.

tier_s_must_memorize_cold.topic: CloudFormation stuck states, policies, and order of operations
tier_s_must_memorize_cold.fact:
ROLLBACK_COMPLETE cannot be updated. The only action is DELETE the stack and recreate. ROLLBACK_FAILED and UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED must be resolved with ContinueUpdateRollback, optionally with ResourcesToSkip.
UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED usually means the resource that failed to roll back was changed outside CloudFormation, or a dependency (e.g. an S3 bucket, a security group in use) blocks it. Fix the underlying resource manually, then ContinueUpdateRollback.
DELETE_FAILED classic causes: non-empty S3 bucket, ENI still attached, security group still referenced, a nested stack in a bad state, or a resource with DeletionPolicy Retain. Empty the bucket, then retry delete with RetainResources for the stuck resource.
An Output Export cannot be deleted or changed while another stack imports it (Fn::ImportValue). Remove the importing stack or the import first - the error reads Export cannot be updated as it is in use by <stack>.
DeletionPolicy (Retain / Snapshot / Delete) applies on stack delete; Snapshot is only valid on resources that can be snapshotted - EBS volume, RDS DB instance, RDS/Aurora DB cluster, ElastiCache cache cluster and replication group, Redshift cluster, Neptune and DocumentDB clusters - everywhere else the only choices are Retain and Delete. UpdateReplacePolicy applies when an update replaces the resource. Both are needed to protect data on both paths. Stack policy = JSON that denies Update:Replace/Delete on specific resources during updates (protects during update, NOT during stack delete). Termination protection blocks stack delete.
CreationPolicy + cfn-signal = wait for the app inside the instance to report success before CloudFormation marks it CREATE_COMPLETE; ResourceSignal Timeout defaults to PT5M (5 minutes), so a long bootstrap must raise it or the create fails. UpdatePolicy on an Auto Scaling group = AutoScalingRollingUpdate / AutoScalingReplacingUpdate.
Template size limits: 51,200 bytes when the template is passed inline in the API request, 1 MB when it is stored in S3 and referenced by URL; 500 resources, 200 parameters, 200 outputs, and 200 mappings per stack - which is why big templates get split into nested stacks.
Change set = preview and see Replacement: True before you break something; drift detection finds manual out-of-band changes but is detect-only and never fixes them. StackSets: self-managed needs AWSCloudFormationStackSetAdministrationRole in the admin account and AWSCloudFormationStackSetExecutionRole in each target; service-managed uses Organizations trusted access and supports automatic deployment to new accounts.

tier_s_must_memorize_cold.topic: EC2 Auto Scaling mechanics and defaults
tier_s_must_memorize_cold.fact:
Default cooldown is 300 seconds and applies to simple scaling policies; target tracking and step scaling use instance warm-up instead, which is the better answer when scaling is too slow.
Health check type defaults to EC2 (instance status checks only). To have the ASG replace instances that the load balancer marks unhealthy, set health check type to ELB. Health check grace period is 300 s when you create the group in the console but 0 by default through the API/CLI/CloudFormation - too short and instances get killed mid-bootstrap, which is the classic instance-churn cause.
Default termination policy order: AZ with most instances (rebalance) -> then the instance with the oldest launch template or launch configuration -> then the instance closest to the next billing hour -> then random. Custom policies: OldestInstance, NewestInstance, OldestLaunchTemplate, AllocationStrategy, plus Lambda-based.
Lifecycle hooks pause instances in Pending:Wait or Terminating:Wait so you can bootstrap or drain; you must CompleteLifecycleAction (or extend it with RecordLifecycleActionHeartbeat) or wait for the heartbeat timeout (default 3,600 s, maximum 172,800 s / 48 h) - a stuck hook looks like instances sitting in Pending:Wait.
Scaling policy types: target tracking (pick a metric and a target value - simplest, default answer), step (scale by amount depending on breach size), simple (single step with cooldown - legacy), scheduled (known time patterns), predictive (ML forecast, needs 24 h of history, best with daily/weekly cycles).
Suspend the AZRebalance, Terminate, Launch, HealthCheck, ReplaceUnhealthy, ScheduledActions, AddToLoadBalancer processes to stop the ASG interfering during maintenance. Standby removes an instance from service without terminating it.
Instance refresh = rolling replacement to a new launch template version, with MinHealthyPercentage (default 90%) and optional checkpoints - the exam answer for immutable/rolling deployment across an ASG. Warm pools cut long boot times. Launch configurations are retired for new use - you cannot create new ones, so any option that says 'create a launch configuration' is wrong; launch templates support versions and every newer feature.

tier_s_must_memorize_cold.topic: ELB 5xx codes, target health, and Route 53 health checks
tier_s_must_memorize_cold.fact:
ALB 503 = no healthy or no registered targets in the target group (or no target group for the rule). ALB 502 = target returned a malformed response, closed the connection, or a Lambda target errored. ALB 504 = target did not respond within the idle timeout (default 60 s). ALB 460 = client closed the connection before the target responded. ALB 400 = malformed client request. HTTP 5xx with ELB 5XX_Count vs Target 5XX_Count tells you whether the LB or the app produced it.
Target health check: protocol, port (traffic-port by default), path, and the 30 / 5 / 5 / 2 defaults - interval 30 s, timeout 5 s, healthy threshold 5, unhealthy threshold 2 - plus the success matcher (default 200 for ALB; NLB matcher 200-399). Health-check failure reasons appear verbatim in the console: Target.Timeout, Target.FailedHealthChecks, Target.ResponseCodeMismatch, Target.NotInUse, Elb.RegistrationInProgress.
The target security group must allow the health-check port FROM the load balancer security group (ALB) or from the VPC/NLB subnet CIDRs (NLB, which preserves client IP and has no SG on the NLB itself by default).
Deregistration delay (connection draining) default 300 s - lower it to speed up deployments, raise it for long-lived requests. ALB idle timeout default 60 s; keep the target keep-alive timeout HIGHER than the ALB idle timeout to avoid 502s.
Cross-zone load balancing: ALB is ON by default and free; NLB and GWLB are OFF by default (and cross-zone data is charged). Uneven load across AZs on an NLB is the cross-zone-off symptom.
Route 53 health checks: types are endpoint, calculated (parent of child checks), and CloudWatch alarm. Failure threshold default 3, request interval 30 s standard or 10 s fast. Health checkers are PUBLIC internet - a private endpoint cannot be checked directly, so publish a metric and use a CloudWatch alarm health check.
Alias records are free, can point at the zone apex, and support Evaluate Target Health; CNAMEs cannot exist at the zone apex. Failover routing needs a health check attached to the primary record.

RDS automated backup retention is 0 to 35 days (0 disables and also disables PITR); manual snapshots persist until you delete them, and survive DB instance deletion. PITR restores to a NEW DB instance with a NEW endpoint - you must repoint the application or move the CNAME. Same for snapshot restore.
DynamoDB PITR gives 35 days of continuous backup and also restores to a NEW table; on-demand backups are retained until deleted and are full backups.
EBS snapshots are incremental but each snapshot is independently restorable - deleting an old snapshot never breaks a newer one. A restored volume is lazy-loaded from S3; Fast Snapshot Restore (FSR) removes that first-touch latency and is enabled per snapshot per AZ (charged per AZ-hour). Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM) automates snapshot/AMI create, copy, retain, and cross-Region copy by tag.
An AMI is an EBS snapshot plus launch metadata. To share an encrypted snapshot or AMI you MUST use a customer managed KMS key and share the key too - snapshots encrypted with the default aws/ebs key cannot be shared.
AWS Backup = central plans (rules: frequency, backup window, lifecycle to cold storage, retention), vaults, resource assignment by tag or resource ID, cross-Region and cross-account copy, Vault Lock in governance mode (a principal with backup:DeleteBackupVaultLockConfiguration can remove it at any time - it never becomes immutable) or compliance mode (deletable only during the cooling-off period you set at creation, minimum 3 days, and immutable to everyone including root after that), Backup Audit Manager for compliance reports, and restore testing.
S3 durability tools: versioning (protects against overwrite/delete), MFA Delete (root-only to enable, blocks version delete), Object Lock in governance or compliance mode (requires versioning, must be enabled ideally at bucket creation), and CRR/SRR replication (needs versioning on both buckets plus an IAM role; replication is not retroactive - use Batch Replication for existing objects).
DR patterns by RTO/RPO and cost: backup and restore (hours, cheapest) -> pilot light (tens of minutes, data replicated, compute off) -> warm standby (minutes, scaled-down live copy) -> multi-site active-active (near zero, most expensive).

tier_s_must_memorize_cold.topic: VPC troubleshooting checklist (run in this order)
tier_s_must_memorize_cold.fact:
Order of checks for any no-connectivity question: 1) route table entry, 2) IGW / NAT / endpoint present and correct, 3) public IP or Elastic IP on the instance, 4) security group (stateful, both directions of the FLOW not the packet), 5) NACL (stateless, needs an explicit return rule on ephemeral ports 1024-65535), 6) OS firewall / app listening, 7) DNS.
Public subnet = a subnet whose route table has 0.0.0.0/0 -> igw-xxxx. An instance also needs a public IPv4 address or EIP. Private subnet reaches the internet outbound only through a NAT gateway that lives in a PUBLIC subnet, with 0.0.0.0/0 -> nat-xxxx in the private route table.
Security groups are stateful (return traffic is automatically allowed) and allow-only - you cannot write a deny rule. NACLs are stateless, evaluated in rule-number order lowest first, and the default NACL allows all while a newly CREATED custom NACL denies all.
Gateway endpoints (S3 and DynamoDB only) are free and require a ROUTE TABLE entry with the prefix list - no ENI, no DNS change, no SG. Interface endpoints (PrivateLink) create an ENI with a security group and need Enable private DNS plus enableDnsSupport and enableDnsHostnames on the VPC to make the public service name resolve privately.
VPC peering is non-transitive, cannot have overlapping CIDRs, needs routes on BOTH sides, and does not support edge-to-edge routing through an IGW/NAT/VGW. Use Transit Gateway for hub-and-spoke and transitive routing (check TGW route tables plus association plus propagation plus the subnet route to the TGW).
Longest-prefix match wins in a route table; the local route always wins for the VPC CIDR and cannot be overridden.
Reachability Analyzer proves whether a path exists and names the blocking component (SG, NACL, route). Network Access Analyzer finds unintended access paths. Flow Logs tell you what actually happened.

Fields to know: version, account-id, interface-id, srcaddr, dstaddr, srcport, dstport, protocol, packets, bytes, start, end, action (ACCEPT or REJECT), log-status (OK, NODATA, SKIPDATA).
The headline rule: inbound ACCEPT recorded but the matching outbound (return) entry shows REJECT means a NACL blocked the return traffic - a security group would never accept in and reject out, because SGs are stateful.
No inbound record at all (only the request missing entirely) means the packet never arrived: check routing, IGW/NAT, or an upstream firewall - Flow Logs only record traffic that reaches an ENI.
Inbound REJECT alone means the security group (or a NACL inbound rule) blocked it on arrival.
log-status NODATA = no traffic during the aggregation window; SKIPDATA = records were skipped due to capacity, not a security event.
Flow Logs do NOT capture: DNS queries to the Amazon-provided resolver (169.254.169.253), instance metadata service 169.254.169.254, DHCP, Amazon Windows license activation, or traffic to the reserved VPC router address. Use Route 53 Resolver query logging for DNS.
Destinations are CloudWatch Logs, S3, or Data Firehose; default aggregation interval 10 minutes, can be set to 1 minute. Flow logs cannot be changed after creation - delete and recreate to modify the format or filter. Query with CloudWatch Logs Insights (CloudWatch destination) or Athena (S3 destination).

Low cache hit ratio is almost always the cache key. Forwarding all headers, all cookies, or all query strings in the cache policy fragments the cache - forward only what the origin actually varies on. Use an origin request policy to pass values to the origin WITHOUT adding them to the cache key.
TTL controls: origin Cache-Control max-age wins between MinTTL and MaxTTL; DefaultTTL (24 hours) applies when the origin sends no caching header, MinTTL defaults to 0 and MaxTTL to 365 days. Cache-Control: no-store or private from the origin means nothing is cached.
Stale content: invalidation (/* or specific paths) purges now but is slow and only 1,000 paths per month are free. Versioned object names (app.v2.js) are the recommended, cheaper answer for controlled releases.
403 from CloudFront with an S3 origin: bucket policy does not allow the Origin Access Control principal, the object does not exist and the bucket denies s3:ListBucket (S3 returns 403 instead of 404), or WAF/geo restriction blocked it. Use OAC (current) rather than legacy OAI, and remember OAC with SSE-KMS needs kms:Decrypt for the CloudFront service principal.
502 from CloudFront = origin SSL/TLS negotiation failure or invalid certificate/cipher; 504 = origin timed out or a security group/firewall blocks the CloudFront edge; 503 = origin capacity.
Certificates: a CloudFront alternate domain name requires an ACM certificate in us-east-1 (N. Virginia). ALB/other regional services need the certificate in their own Region.
Other levers: origin failover with an origin group (fails over on defined 4xx/5xx), geo restriction, signed URLs (one object) vs signed cookies (many objects), field-level encryption, compression (must also allow the client to signal Accept-Encoding), Price Classes to limit edge locations, CloudFront Functions (viewer request/response, sub-ms, header/URL manipulation) vs Lambda@Edge (all four triggers, can call other services and access the body).

tier_s_must_memorize_cold.topic: IAM, SCPs, Config, and Trusted Advisor
tier_s_must_memorize_cold.fact:
Policy evaluation: explicit DENY always wins -> then an explicit ALLOW -> otherwise implicit deny. For cross-account access BOTH the identity policy in the caller account and the resource policy (or role trust policy) in the target account must allow. An SCP never GRANTS permission, it only sets the maximum boundary; a permissions boundary likewise only caps, it never grants.
Troubleshooting access denied, in order: read the error message (it names the principal, action, and resource), check CloudTrail for the exact denied API call, run the IAM policy simulator, run IAM Access Analyzer (external access findings; unused access findings for stale roles/permissions), check SCPs, permissions boundaries, session policies, and resource policies, then check KMS key policy if encryption is involved.
Useful condition keys: aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent, aws:SourceIp, aws:PrincipalOrgID, aws:RequestedRegion (Region restriction), aws:SecureTransport (force HTTPS), aws:PrincipalTag / aws:ResourceTag (ABAC), s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption.
Config records resource configuration over time and evaluates rules (AWS managed or custom via Lambda / Guard). Conformance packs bundle rules plus remediation as a deployable unit; an aggregator gives multi-account multi-Region views. Auto-remediation in Config is wired to a Systems Manager AUTOMATION document - that is the exam default (a Lambda can be invoked, but only as a step inside Automation or via EventBridge).
Config answers what changed and was it compliant. CloudTrail answers who called what API and when. CloudWatch answers is it healthy and performing.
Trusted Advisor categories: cost optimization, performance, security, fault tolerance, service limits (quotas), operational excellence. All checks require Business, Enterprise On-Ramp, or Enterprise Support; Basic/Developer only get the free core security and service-quota checks (S3 bucket permissions, security groups with unrestricted specific ports, IAM use, MFA on root account, public EBS/RDS snapshots, exposed access keys).
Other guardrails: Organizations SCPs and RCPs, Control Tower preventive/detective/proactive controls, IAM Identity Center permission sets for federated human access (do not create IAM users for humans), and a credential report / access advisor for stale credentials.

KMS key types: AWS owned (invisible, no control), AWS managed aws/<service> (rotated every year, key policy not editable, CANNOT be shared cross-account), and customer managed (CMK - editable key policy, optional automatic rotation on a configurable period from 90 to 2,560 days plus on-demand rotation you can trigger yourself, cross-account sharing, scheduled deletion with a 7 to 30 day waiting period, default 30). KMS HSMs are validated to FIPS 140-3 Level 3, which is the answer to any 'validated hardware key store' stem that does not require CloudHSM.
A KMS key policy must exist and must at minimum grant the account root so IAM policies can take effect - a key policy that does not delegate to IAM makes every IAM grant useless. Cross-account use needs BOTH the key policy in the owning account AND an IAM policy in the using account.
You cannot encrypt an existing unencrypted EBS volume in place. The path is: snapshot -> copy the snapshot with Encrypted=true and a KMS key -> create a volume from the encrypted copy -> attach. Same idea for AMIs. Encryption by default can be enabled per Region per account.
RDS encryption can only be enabled at CREATE time; to encrypt an existing unencrypted DB, snapshot it, copy the snapshot with encryption, and restore. You cannot remove encryption from an encrypted DB.
KMS ThrottlingException under load = raise a quota increase, add exponential backoff, or use S3 Bucket Keys / DEK caching to reduce KMS calls.
ACM: DNS validation auto-renews indefinitely as long as the CNAME record stays and the certificate is in use; EMAIL validation does NOT auto-renew silently - it needs manual action every 13 months. IMPORTED certificates never auto-renew - watch the ACM expiry EventBridge event / Config rule. A public ACM certificate is valid 13 months and ACM begins attempting renewal 60 days before expiry. Certificates are regional; CloudFront requires us-east-1. Since June 2025 ACM can issue EXPORTABLE public certificates (certificate, chain, and private key, priced per FQDN, 395-day validity, and the exportable flag must be set at request time) for EC2, on-premises, or other clouds - ordinary free ACM certificates still cannot be exported and only attach to integrated AWS services.
Secrets Manager vs Parameter Store: Secrets Manager costs roughly $0.40 per secret per month plus API calls and holds up to 64 KB per secret, supports built-in automatic ROTATION (managed rotation for RDS, Aurora, Redshift, and DocumentDB needs NO Lambda function of your own - only non-managed targets need a rotation Lambda), cross-account resource policies, and cross-Region replication. Parameter Store SecureString is free (standard tier), integrates with CloudFormation and SSM, but has no native rotation. Rotation requirement in the stem = Secrets Manager.

Multi-AZ standby is NOT readable and serves no traffic - it exists only for failover (60 to 120 s typical) and the writer ENDPOINT stays the same, so an app that fails after failover has a stale DNS cache / JVM TTL problem, not an RDS problem. Read replicas serve reads, are asynchronous, have their own endpoint, and can be cross-Region; promoting a replica breaks replication and creates a standalone instance; the limit is 15 read replicas for MySQL, MariaDB, and PostgreSQL but only 5 for SQL Server and Oracle. Multi-AZ DB cluster is the hybrid: two standbys that ARE readable and a failover of typically under 35 seconds, versus 60-120 s and no readable standby for a Multi-AZ DB instance.
Performance Insights = database-internal load: DB load in Average Active Sessions, top SQL, top waits, top hosts/users. Enhanced Monitoring = OS-level metrics from an agent on the host at 1 to 60 second granularity (process list, per-process CPU/memory) delivered to CloudWatch Logs. Question mentions OS process or per-process memory -> Enhanced Monitoring. Question mentions slow query / wait events / top SQL -> Performance Insights.
CloudWatch RDS metrics to know: CPUUtilization, FreeableMemory, FreeStorageSpace, DatabaseConnections, ReadIOPS/WriteIOPS, ReadLatency/WriteLatency, ReplicaLag, BurstBalance (gp2), DiskQueueDepth, SwapUsage.
Parameter groups: dynamic parameters apply immediately; STATIC parameters require a manual reboot of the instance to take effect (pending-reboot status). You cannot edit the default parameter group - create a custom one, associate it, then reboot. Option groups are for engine features (Oracle TDE, SQL Server native backup).
Storage: storage autoscaling raises allocated storage automatically up to the maximum threshold you set, and it triggers only when free space drops below 10% of allocated storage, stays there for at least 5 minutes, and at least 6 hours have passed since the last storage modification; storage-full is a hard stop that puts the instance in storage-full state. You cannot shrink RDS storage. There is a 6-hour cooldown between storage modifications.
RDS Proxy pools and multiplexes connections - the answer when Lambda or a bursty app exhausts DatabaseConnections, and it also shortens failover time and holds credentials in Secrets Manager.
Backups: automated backups 0-35 days with a backup window; PITR to any second in the window, restoring to a NEW instance with a NEW endpoint. Events (failover, low storage, backup) publish to SNS via RDS event subscriptions. Maintenance window applies engine patches; Multi-AZ patches the standby first, then fails over, reducing downtime. Aurora: up to 15 read replicas sharing one storage volume, failover priority tiers 0-15 (lowest tier promoted first), reader/writer/custom endpoints, Backtrack (MySQL) rewinds without restore, Aurora Serverless v2 scales in 0.5 ACU increments.

D1.fact: Config wizard produces a JSON stored in Parameter Store (default name AmazonCloudWatch-*); deploy fleet-wide with SSM Run Command document AWS-ConfigureAWSPackage plus AmazonCloudWatch-ManageAgent. Agent collects memory, disk, swap, procstat, and any log file.

Metrics retention: 1-second (high-resolution) data 3 hours, 1-minute data 15 days, 5-minute data 63 days, 1-hour data 455 days (15 months). Data is aggregated as it ages, never deleted outright. Sub-1-minute data disappears fast - alarm on it quickly or export.

Average hides spikes; use Maximum for saturation, Sum for counts (RequestCount, Invocations), p90/p99 percentile for latency SLOs, SampleCount for volume. Period must be at least the metric publishing interval or the alarm sees gaps.

Treat missing data as: notBreaching (treat as OK), breaching (treat as ALARM), ignore (keep current state), missing (default - alarm evaluates on available data, may go INSUFFICIENT_DATA). Instances that scale to zero need notBreaching or ignore.

Composite alarm rule syntax ALARM(child1) AND ALARM(child2). Used to reduce alert noise and to send one page instead of twenty. Composite alarms can have their own SNS action and an actions-suppressor for maintenance.

Metric filter turns log patterns into a CloudWatch metric you can alarm on (no historical backfill). Subscription filter streams log events in near real time to Lambda, Data Firehose, Kinesis Data Streams, or OpenSearch - and you can attach only 2 subscription filters to a single log group, so a third consumer means fanning out through Firehose or Lambda. Filter pattern syntax differs for JSON ({$.errorCode = "AccessDenied"}) vs plain text.

Query language with fields, filter, stats, sort, limit, parse. Example: fields @timestamp, @message | filter @message like /ERROR/ | stats count() by bin(5m). Queries a maximum of 50 log groups (or use a log group class/pattern); results retained 7 days.

CloudWatch cross-account observability links monitoring accounts (sink) to source accounts (link) to view metrics, logs, and traces centrally. Cross-account cross-Region dashboards require the sharing role CloudWatch-CrossAccountSharingRole.

Canaries run Node/Python scripts on a schedule from outside your app to test availability, broken links, API workflows, and page load - the answer for 'detect an outage before customers report it' and for monitoring endpoints Route 53 cannot reach. Canaries can run inside a VPC.

Container Insights gives ECS/EKS cluster, node, pod, and task metrics plus performance logs (EKS needs the CloudWatch Observability add-on). Application Signals gives service-level SLOs, latency, and fault rates with automatic service maps. Managed Service for Prometheus + Managed Grafana for open-source Prometheus workloads.

Management events (control-plane, logged free once per Region) vs data events (S3 object-level, Lambda invoke, DynamoDB item - NOT logged by default, extra cost) vs Insights events (unusual API call-rate or error-rate). Missing s3:GetObject in CloudTrail = data events not enabled.

Log file validation produces digest files so you can prove logs were not altered. An organization trail captures all member accounts into one bucket and members cannot disable it. CloudTrail Event history is the free, always-on 90-day console record of management events in each Region - anything older, or any data event, needs a trail or a CloudTrail Lake event data store. CloudTrail Lake gives SQL queries over event data stores with retention configurable up to 10 years.

Rule does not fire -> event pattern mismatch (patterns are exact JSON match, case-sensitive; use the Sandbox to test) or the event is on a different bus. Rule fires but nothing happens -> target permissions (resource policy for Lambda/SNS/SQS, IAM role for API targets). The default target retry policy is 24 hours and 185 attempts; add an SQS dead-letter queue on the target so the events that still fail are visible instead of silently dropped. A rule can have at most 5 targets - more than that means fanning out through SNS or a second rule. Archive plus replay to reprocess.
EventBridge Scheduler = one-time or recurring schedules at scale (millions), with flexible time windows, time zones, and retries - the modern replacement for rules with cron for scheduled invocation.

Standard exam chain: CloudWatch alarm or Config rule or GuardDuty finding -> EventBridge rule -> SSM Automation runbook (or Lambda) -> fix and notify via SNS. Prefer SSM Automation over custom Lambda when the stem says least operational overhead.

Needs at least 30 hours of CloudWatch metrics within the last 14 days to make a recommendation; enable memory metrics via the CloudWatch agent for accurate rightsizing. Covers EC2, ASGs, EBS, Lambda, ECS on Fargate, RDS. Cost Explorer rightsizing recommendations overlap but are cost-first.

VolumeQueueLength high with high latency = the volume is the bottleneck. BurstBalance dropping to 0 on gp2/st1/sc1 = burst credits exhausted (slow-down symptom). gp3 decouples IOPS/throughput from size; io2 Block Express for high IOPS with durability; st1/sc1 for large sequential throughput, never for boot volumes.

You can modify size, type, and IOPS online, but there is a 6-hour cooling-off period before you can modify the same volume again, and volumes may sit in optimizing state while still usable. Shrinking is not possible - create a smaller volume and copy.

S3 scales to at least 3,500 PUT/COPY/POST/DELETE and 5,500 GET/HEAD requests per second per prefix. Use multipart upload for objects over 100 MB (required over 5 GB), byte-range fetches for parallel downloads, Transfer Acceleration for long-distance uploads over the CloudFront edge network, and DataSync for bulk online transfer with validation and scheduling.

EFS: Elastic throughput is the default modern choice; Bursting uses BurstCreditBalance (draining to zero = throughput throttling). Lifecycle management moves files to IA/Archive after a set idle period. FSx for Windows = SMB/AD; FSx for Lustre = HPC and S3-linked; FSx for NetApp ONTAP = multiprotocol. FSx for OpenZFS is explicitly out of scope for SOA-C03 - if it appears as an option it is a distractor.

D2.fact: Min / max / desired. Desired capacity is what the ASG maintains now; scaling policies move desired between min and max. If desired is already at max, no scaling policy will help - the exam symptom is 'the alarm fired but no instances launched'.

Slow to respond to spikes -> reduce alarm period / use detailed monitoring (1-min), reduce cooldown or set an instance warm-up, use target tracking instead of simple, use step scaling for large steps, or use warm pools / predictive scaling for known patterns.

Capacity Rebalancing proactively replaces Spot instances that receive a rebalance recommendation before the 2-minute interruption notice. Mixed instances policy with multiple instance types and the price-capacity-optimized allocation strategy reduces interruption risk.

Service Auto Scaling uses Application Auto Scaling with target tracking on ECSServiceAverageCPUUtilization, ECSServiceAverageMemoryUtilization, or ALBRequestCountPerTarget. Cluster capacity providers with managed scaling scale the EC2 capacity behind the tasks; Fargate needs no capacity management.

HPA scales pods on metrics (needs metrics-server), Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter scales nodes, VPA rightsizes pod requests. Pods stuck Pending = no node capacity or no matching IP addresses in the subnet (VPC CNI IP exhaustion).

On-demand for unpredictable traffic (no capacity planning; it instantly absorbs up to double the previous peak, and a bigger jump than that needs pre-warming or provisioned capacity); provisioned plus auto scaling with a target utilization (default 70%) for predictable. Hot partition / throttling = poor partition key design; ProvisionedThroughputExceededException plus ThrottledRequests metric. DAX gives microsecond reads for read-heavy eventually consistent workloads.

CloudFront for edge/static and dynamic HTTP; ElastiCache (Redis/Valkey for persistence, replicas, pub/sub; Memcached for simple multi-threaded caching) for database offload; DAX only for DynamoDB. Cache to fix repeated identical reads, not to fix a bad query plan.

Aurora supports up to 15 read replicas; a reader endpoint round-robins connections across them. Aurora Auto Scaling adds replicas on target metrics. Aurora Serverless v2 scales capacity in 0.5 ACU increments in place, without dropping connections.

ALB = layer 7, host/path/header/query routing, WAF integration, Lambda and IP targets, HTTP 5xx codes. NLB = layer 4, ultra-low latency, static IP per AZ / EIP support, preserves client IP, TLS passthrough, PrivateLink service front end. GWLB = layer 3 for third-party inspection appliances using GENEVE 6081.

ALB duration-based stickiness uses the AWSALB cookie; application-based stickiness uses your own cookie. Stickiness causes uneven target load and prevents graceful scale-in - the symptom is 'one instance is hot after scaling out'.

Failover is triggered by AZ failure, instance failure, storage failure, instance-type change, or OS patching, and by a manual reboot-with-failover. A Multi-AZ DB INSTANCE takes 60-120 s and its standby is not readable; a Multi-AZ DB CLUSTER fails over in under 35 s and its two standbys are readable. The endpoint is unchanged - the CNAME repoints. Applications that cache DNS forever (Java networkaddress.cache.ttl) must set a short TTL.

Simple (no health check), weighted (gradual/blue-green shift), latency (lowest network latency Region), failover (active-passive with health check), geolocation (by user location, compliance), geoproximity (bias toward a Region, needs traffic flow), multivalue answer (up to 8 healthy records, poor-man's LB), IP-based (by client CIDR).

A private hosted zone resolves only inside associated VPCs and requires enableDnsSupport AND enableDnsHostnames on the VPC. Route 53 public health checkers cannot reach private resources - use a CloudWatch alarm health check instead.

Global Accelerator gives two static anycast IPs, works for TCP/UDP and non-HTTP protocols, does instant regional failover on health checks, and does not cache. CloudFront caches HTTP(S) content at edges. Static IP requirement or gaming/VoIP -> Global Accelerator.

A backup plan has rules (schedule with cron, backup window, lifecycle transition to cold storage - minimum 90 days in cold, retention) and a resource assignment (by tag or resource ID). Copy actions send recovery points to another Region or account vault. Restores create new resources; test them with restore testing plans.

Governance mode: a principal with backup:DeleteBackupVaultLockConfiguration can remove the lock at any time - there is no cooling-off period and it never becomes immutable, so it is a guardrail against mistakes, not a regulator. Compliance mode: you set a cooling-off period of at least 3 days (ChangeableForDays) when you create the lock; during it the lock can still be deleted, and once it expires nobody, including the root user or AWS, can delete the lock, shorten retention, or delete recovery points. Regulatory WORM requirement -> compliance mode.

Copying a snapshot cross-Region re-encrypts with a destination-Region key. AMIs are Region-scoped - a launch template referencing an AMI ID fails in another Region. Use Image Builder distribution or DLM cross-Region copy to keep AMIs in sync.

RTO = how long until service is restored (drives architecture: standby capacity). RPO = how much data you can lose (drives backup frequency/replication). Continuous replication -> seconds RPO; nightly snapshot -> up to 24 h RPO.

ARC zonal shift moves traffic away from an impaired Availability Zone for ALB/NLB with one action (zonal autoshift lets AWS do it automatically). Readiness checks verify that recovery Regions are actually ready; routing controls are on/off switches wired to Route 53 health checks for deliberate failover.

D2.topic: Health check grace period and churn
D2.fact: If instances repeatedly launch and terminate, look at (a) ELB health check type with a grace period shorter than bootstrap, (b) a failing health-check path, (c) an incorrect AMI/user data crash, (d) a lifecycle hook timing out, (e) Spot interruptions, (f) subnet IP exhaustion preventing launch.

D3.fact: Sections: AWSTemplateFormatVersion, Description, Metadata, Parameters, Mappings, Conditions, Transform, Resources (the only required section), Outputs. Transform: AWS::Serverless (SAM) or AWS::Include.

Ref (parameter value or resource default ID), Fn::GetAtt (resource attribute like an ARN or DNS name), Fn::Sub (string interpolation), Fn::Join, Fn::FindInMap (region-to-AMI Mappings), Fn::ImportValue (cross-stack), Fn::If/Equals/Not (Conditions), Fn::Select/Split, Fn::Cidr, Fn::GetAZs. Pseudo parameters: AWS::Region, AWS::AccountId, AWS::StackName, AWS::Partition, AWS::NoValue.

Nested stacks = reusable components owned by one parent, updated together (AWS::CloudFormation::Stack). Cross-stack exports = loose coupling between independently owned stacks, but an export in use blocks both deletion and modification. Choose nested for shared reusable modules, exports for shared long-lived infrastructure like a VPC.

AWS::CloudFormation::CustomResource or Custom::Name backed by a Lambda or SNS topic. The Lambda MUST send a SUCCESS/FAILED response to the pre-signed URL or the stack hangs in CREATE_IN_PROGRESS until the 1-hour timeout - the classic hung-stack cause.

Give CloudFormation a service role so it uses those permissions instead of the caller's; this lets operators deploy stacks without holding the underlying resource permissions. Stack failing with AccessDenied on a resource type = the service role (or caller) lacks that create permission.

Insufficient subnet IP addresses, an AMI ID that does not exist in that Region, a resource limit/quota exceeded, an IAM role not yet propagated, an S3 bucket name already taken globally, or a security group in the wrong VPC. Read the Events tab bottom-up - the FIRST failure is the real cause.

Set OnFailure=DO_NOTHING or disable rollback to keep failed resources for debugging instead of dropping to ROLLBACK_COMPLETE. Preserve-successfully-provisioned-resources retries the update from where it failed.

A stack set deploys one template to many accounts and Regions. Self-managed permissions need the administration role in the admin account and the execution role in each target. Service-managed uses Organizations, supports deploying to OUs and auto-deployment to newly created accounts. Operation preferences control failure tolerance and max concurrent accounts; drift detection also works on stack sets.

CDK synthesizes to CloudFormation (cdk synth) and deploys via CloudFormation (cdk deploy). cdk bootstrap creates the CDKToolkit stack with the staging bucket/ECR repo and roles - deploy failures in a new account/Region are almost always missing bootstrap. Constructs L1 (Cfn*) / L2 (opinionated) / L3 (patterns).

Pipeline = recipe (base image + components) + infrastructure configuration + distribution configuration + schedule. Components are YAML build/test/validate steps. Distribution copies and shares AMIs across Regions and accounts. Answer for 'automate golden AMI creation and patching'.

Basic scanning is free and CVE-based on push; enhanced scanning uses Amazon Inspector for continuous OS and language-package scanning. Lifecycle policies expire old images; cross-Region/cross-account replication; pull-through cache for upstream registries; login via aws ecr get-login-password (12-hour token).

In-place/rolling (cheapest, mixed versions), blue-green (two environments, switch via ALB weighted target groups or Route 53 weighted records - instant rollback), canary (small percentage first, e.g. Lambda alias weights), immutable (new instances only, via ASG instance refresh or a new ASG), linear/all-at-once for Lambda and ECS via CodeDeploy.

minimumHealthyPercent and maximumPercent govern rolling updates: 100/200 replaces without capacity loss, 50/100 replaces in place using existing capacity. Circuit breaker with rollback aborts and reverts a failing deployment automatically.

Patch baseline defines approval rules (classification, severity, auto-approval delay) and exceptions; patch group is a TAG with key 'Patch Group'; Maintenance Window schedules the scan/install with a registered task and target. Compliance reporting shows non-compliant nodes. AWS-RunPatchBaseline is the document.

D3.topic: State Manager vs Automation vs Run Command
D3.fact: Run Command = do it now, once. State Manager = keep it this way, repeatedly, on a schedule. Automation = a multi-step workflow with branching, approvals, and AWS API calls. Trigger words: 'ensure/enforce/continuously' -> State Manager; 'remediate/runbook/multi-step' -> Automation; 'ad hoc on N instances' -> Run Command.

SecureString needs kms:Decrypt on the key plus ssm:GetParameter. Path hierarchies (/prod/app/db/password) allow GetParametersByPath with recursion and IAM scoping by path. Parameter policies (expiration, ExpirationNotification, NoChangeNotification) are Advanced tier only; changes emit EventBridge events.

S3 Event Notifications go to SNS, SQS, Lambda, or EventBridge. Use EventBridge for richer filtering, multiple targets, and cross-account routing. Notification not firing -> missing resource policy on the target, wrong prefix/suffix filter, or overlapping notification configurations.

AWS Resource Access Manager shares subnets (VPC sharing), Transit Gateways, Route 53 Resolver rules, License Manager configurations, and IPAM pools across accounts in an organization. Sharing a subnet means the participant launches resources into the owner's VPC; the owner still manages route tables, NACLs, and the IGW.

Portfolios contain products (CloudFormation templates) with launch constraints (a role users assume so they need no underlying permissions), template constraints (restrict parameter values), and tag options. The answer for 'let teams self-serve approved infrastructure without broad IAM'.

Terraform state must be remote and locked for teams (S3 backend plus DynamoDB or S3 native locking). terraform plan is the change-set equivalent. Git: feature branch -> PR -> review -> merge to main; never commit credentials; use tags for release versions.

D4.fact: Account password policy sets minimum length (default 8, up to 128), character requirements, rotation (max 1,095 days), reuse prevention (up to 24), and whether users may change their own password. Enforce MFA with a policy condition on aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent plus a self-service exception for managing their own MFA device.

Enable MFA on root, delete root access keys, never use root for daily work; Organizations centralized root access management can remove root credentials from member accounts. Trusted Advisor and Security Hub both flag root MFA missing.

EC2 gets an instance profile role; Lambda gets an execution role; ECS tasks get a task role (task execution role is for pulling images and writing logs); EKS pods use IRSA or EKS Pod Identity. Hardcoded access keys on an instance is always the wrong answer.

Create a role in the target account with a trust policy naming the source account/principal (optionally with an ExternalId for third parties), grant sts:AssumeRole in the source account. Resource-based policies (S3, KMS, SQS, Lambda) can grant directly without assuming a role.

Central workforce SSO with an identity source (Identity Center directory, Active Directory, or external IdP via SAML/SCIM), permission sets that materialize as roles in each account, and attribute-based access via session tags. The correct answer for federated human access at scale.

External access findings show resources shared outside your zone of trust (account or organization). Unused access findings surface unused roles, users, and permissions for least-privilege cleanup. Policy validation and custom policy checks run in CI. Access Analyzer can also generate a policy from CloudTrail activity.

Policy simulator answers 'would this call be allowed' before it happens (does not evaluate resource policies fully in every case). CloudTrail answers 'why was this call denied' after it happened - the errorCode AccessDenied event carries the principal, action, and often the explicit reason.

SCPs apply to member accounts (never the management account) and filter permissions for IAM users/roles in those accounts - they do NOT grant anything and do not apply to service-linked roles. A policy document is capped at 5,120 characters, which is why real-world SCPs are split across several attached policies. Common patterns: deny outside approved Regions with aws:RequestedRegion, deny leaving the organization, deny disabling CloudTrail/GuardDuty/Config, require tags on create.

Resource control policies (RCPs) cap what resource-based policies can grant across the org (e.g. block access from outside the org with aws:PrincipalOrgID). Control Tower controls come in preventive (SCP), detective (Config rule), and proactive (CloudFormation hook) flavours, organized as mandatory / strongly recommended / elective.

Managed rules cover most exam scenarios (required-tags, s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited, encrypted-volumes, restricted-ssh, iam-password-policy). Custom rules use Lambda or Guard. Triggers: configuration change, periodic, or hybrid. Conformance packs bundle rules and remediation for a standard (CIS, PCI, HIPAA).

Attach a remediation action to a non-compliant rule; the action is an SSM Automation document, executed automatically or on demand, with an assume role. Auto-remediation retries are configurable. Example: s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited -> AWS-DisableS3BucketPublicReadWrite.

Aggregates findings in AWS Security Finding Format (ASFF) from GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, IAM Access Analyzer, Config, Firewall Manager, Health, and partners; runs standards (AWS Foundational Security Best Practices, CIS, PCI DSS, NIST) producing a security score; supports cross-Region aggregation, automation rules, and insights. Findings route to EventBridge for remediation.

Agentless threat detection reading CloudTrail management events, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS logs by default, with optional protection plans for S3 data events, EKS audit logs, EC2 malware scanning, RDS login activity, and Lambda network activity. It never needs those logs to be enabled by you. Findings -> EventBridge -> Lambda/SSM remediation. Suppression rules reduce noise.

Continuous vulnerability scanning: EC2 (via SSM agent, or agentless for supported OSes), ECR container images, and Lambda functions/layers. Produces CVE findings with an Inspector risk score and remediation guidance. Requires SSM managed-node status for agent-based EC2 scanning - another reason the SSM prerequisites matter.

Discovers and classifies sensitive data (PII, credentials, financial) in S3, reports bucket-level public/encryption posture, and publishes findings to Security Hub and EventBridge. The answer whenever the stem says 'identify sensitive data in S3'.

AccessDeniedException on decrypt -> key policy or IAM missing kms:Decrypt, or the key is in another account without a matching key policy. KMSKeyNotAccessibleException on ASG launch -> the ASG service-linked role was not granted use of the CMK for the encrypted AMI/snapshot. Key in PendingDeletion state -> cancel deletion (7-30 day window) or the data is unrecoverable. Disabled key -> enable it.

SSE-S3 (AES-256, AWS-managed, default on all new objects), SSE-KMS (auditable via CloudTrail, supports Bucket Keys to cut KMS cost/throttling), DSSE-KMS (dual-layer), SSE-C (you supply the key each request), client-side. Enforce with a bucket policy denying PutObject without the required s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption header, and deny non-TLS with aws:SecureTransport false.

ACM emits Certificate Approaching Expiration EventBridge events (45 days by default) and publishes the DaysToExpiry CloudWatch metric; the Config rule acm-certificate-expiration-check flags them. Imported and email-validated certificates are the ones that actually expire.

D4.topic: WAF, Shield, Network Firewall, DNS Firewall
D4.fact: WAF = layer 7 web ACL on CloudFront, ALB, API Gateway, AppSync, Cognito; managed rule groups, rate-based rules (per 5-minute window per IP), geo match, logging to Firehose/S3/CloudWatch Logs. Shield Standard is free L3/L4; Shield Advanced adds DDoS cost protection, the response team, and health-based detection. Network Firewall = stateful VPC-level IPS with Suricata rules. Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall = block/alert on DNS queries to bad domains.

D4.topic: AWS Security Agent and DevOps Agent framing
D4.fact: Treat the newest agents conservatively: AWS Security Agent = AI agent that assists with security findings and testing; AWS DevOps Agent = AI agent for operational analysis and automated remediation; Kiro = agentic IDE that can generate IaC and scripts. They appear as plausible options; the discriminating fact in a question is almost always the classic service.

D5.fact: AWS reserves 5 IP addresses in every subnet: network address, VPC router, DNS, future use, broadcast. A /28 (16 addresses) yields 11 usable and is the smallest allowed; /16 is the largest subnet and the largest VPC CIDR block. Failed launches with InsufficientFreeAddressesInSubnet = grow the subnet is impossible; add a new subnet or a secondary CIDR to the VPC.

The local route for the VPC CIDR is always present and cannot be removed or overridden. Longest prefix match wins (10.0.1.0/24 beats 10.0.0.0/16 beats 0.0.0.0/0). Each subnet uses the main route table unless explicitly associated with a custom one - a 'suddenly no internet' change is often a lost explicit association.

NAT GW is AZ-scoped, needs an EIP, must sit in a PUBLIC subnet with a route to the IGW, and is not a security boundary. It supports 55,000 concurrent connections per unique destination (same IP, port, and protocol) and scales to 100 Gbps, and it drops idle flows after 350 seconds - so long-lived idle connections need application keep-alives below that. ErrorPortAllocation / IdleTimeoutCount metrics indicate port exhaustion. For HA put one NAT GW per AZ and route each private subnet to its own AZ's NAT. Private NAT gateway handles VPC-to-VPC overlapping-free private routing without internet.

A NAT instance must have source/destination check DISABLED and its own security group; it is a single point of failure and is limited by instance bandwidth. NAT GW is the default answer unless the stem demands port forwarding or a bastion role.
IPv6 addresses are all public, so outbound-only IPv6 internet access uses an egress-only internet gateway (route ::/0 -> eigw-). NAT gateway does not do IPv6 in that role.

Security group: instance level, stateful, allow rules only, all rules evaluated, can reference other security groups. NACL: subnet level, stateless, allow and deny, evaluated in numeric order, must allow ephemeral ports 1024-65535 for return traffic. If you need to block a single malicious IP, only a NACL can deny.

Gateway endpoint: S3 and DynamoDB only, free, route-table based, cannot be reached from on-premises or across peering. Interface endpoint (PrivateLink): ENI with a private IP and security group, hourly plus per-GB charge, reachable from on-premises over Site-to-Site VPN and from other VPCs over peering or Transit Gateway, needs private DNS enabled (or use the endpoint-specific DNS name).

Both endpoint types carry a resource policy that restricts which resources can be reached through the endpoint (e.g. only your buckets). A bucket policy can require aws:SourceVpce to force all access through the endpoint. Access denied through an endpoint that works publicly = the endpoint policy.

Publish a service with an NLB (or GWLB) plus an endpoint service, accept connections from consumer accounts by allowlisting principals. Traffic is one-way (consumer to provider), no route tables, no CIDR overlap concerns - the answer for SaaS or shared internal services across accounts with overlapping IP space.

Non-transitive, no overlapping CIDRs, no edge-to-edge routing (cannot use the peer's IGW, NAT, VPN, or gateway endpoint). Routes required on both sides; security groups can reference peer security groups only in the same Region. Inter-Region peering supports security group references only in limited configurations - default to CIDR rules.

Hub-and-spoke with attachments (VPC, Site-to-Site VPN, TGW peering - and a Direct Connect gateway, which is background context only since Direct Connect is not on the SOA-C03 in-scope list) and TGW route tables using association (which route table an attachment uses) and propagation (which routes get advertised). Isolation between spokes is achieved with separate route tables. Appliance mode keeps flow symmetry for inspection VPCs. Also check the SUBNET route table pointing to the TGW - the most missed step.

Each connection has two tunnels to two endpoints for redundancy; the customer gateway must initiate (NAT-T UDP 4500 / IKE UDP 500) or you must enable DPD/keepalive. Static routes or BGP with a VGW or a Transit Gateway. Accelerated VPN uses Global Accelerator. Tunnel down -> check IKE parameters, pre-shared key, customer-gateway public IP, and firewall rules.

INBOUND endpoint = on-premises queries resolve names IN the VPC (traffic comes IN to AWS). OUTBOUND endpoint plus forwarding rules = VPC queries resolve names ON-PREMISES (traffic goes OUT). Share rules across accounts with RAM. The Amazon-provided resolver is at VPC base +2 and 169.254.169.253.

Route 53 Resolver query logging captures VPC DNS queries to CloudWatch Logs, S3, or Data Firehose. Public hosted zone query logging goes to CloudWatch Logs in us-east-1 only. VPC Flow Logs do not show DNS queries to the Amazon resolver.

D5.topic: CloudFront cache key vs origin request
D5.fact: Cache policy defines the cache key (which headers, cookies, query strings are part of the key) and TTLs. Origin request policy defines what is FORWARDED to the origin without affecting the key. Response headers policy adds CORS/security headers without touching the origin.

Standard logs (v2) deliver to S3, CloudWatch Logs, or Data Firehose with configurable fields; real-time logs stream to Kinesis Data Streams within seconds for live dashboards. The x-edge-result-type field (Hit, Miss, RefreshHit, Error, LimitExceeded) is how you measure and diagnose hit ratio.

Disabled by default; when enabled they land in S3 (5-minute intervals) and need a bucket policy allowing the ELB account or the logdelivery service principal. They contain client IP, target processing time, and the elb_status_code vs target_status_code pair that separates LB errors from app errors. Connection logs (ALB) capture TLS handshake details.

D5.topic: Reachability Analyzer vs Network Access Analyzer
D5.fact: Reachability Analyzer tests a specific source-to-destination path and names the blocking component (the exact security group, NACL, or missing route) - the fastest answer to 'why can't A reach B' without sending traffic, and the one named on the SOA-C03 in-scope service list. Network Access Analyzer evaluates whether unintended network access paths exist against a scope (compliance-style); treat it as the compliance-sweep tool, not the troubleshooting answer.

Internet Monitor shows internet health and performance impact on your users by city/ISP. Network Monitor gives active probes between VPC resources and on-premises destinations with packet loss and latency metrics. Traffic Mirroring copies packets from an ENI to an appliance for deep inspection.

Data transfer out to internet and cross-AZ traffic cost money; same-AZ private IP traffic is free. NAT gateway charges per hour plus per GB - route S3/DynamoDB through free gateway endpoints instead of the NAT to cut cost. CloudFront egress is cheaper than direct EC2/S3 egress and origin-to-edge transfer is free. Interface endpoints cost per hour per AZ, so consolidate.

decision_tables.title: ALB / NLB error codes and target health
rows: HTTP 503 Service Unavailable
No healthy or no registered targets in the target group
Target group Targets tab health status and reason (Target.NotInUse, Target.FailedHealthChecks); HTTPCode_ELB_503_Count metric
Register targets, fix the failing health check, or correct the listener rule that points to an empty target group
HTTP 502 Bad Gateway
Target returned a malformed response, reset the connection, or a Lambda target errored/returned bad JSON
Access logs target_status_code = -; application logs; target keep-alive timeout vs ALB idle timeout; TLS cipher mismatch on HTTPS targets
Set the target keep-alive timeout above 60 s, fix the app response, fix the Lambda response format, or fix the backend certificate
HTTP 504 Gateway Timeout
Target did not respond within the ALB idle timeout (default 60 s)
TargetResponseTime metric; slow queries; whether the target SG allows the ALB SG on the traffic port
Speed up the backend, raise the idle timeout, or fix the SG/NACL path so packets actually arrive
HTTP 460
Client closed the connection before the target responded
Client-side timeouts; TargetResponseTime near client timeout
Reduce backend latency or raise the client timeout - not an ALB fault
Malformed request, bad X-Forwarded-For, or protocol version mismatch (HTTP/2 to HTTP/1 target)
Access log request line; listener protocol version setting
Correct the client request or set the correct backend protocol version
Targets flapping healthy/unhealthy
Health check interval/threshold too aggressive or the health path does real work
The 30 / 5 / 5 / 2 defaults - interval 30 s, timeout 5 s, healthy threshold 5, unhealthy threshold 2 - and matcher 200
Use a lightweight /health path, widen the threshold, and lengthen the timeout
All targets unhealthy but the app works via SSH
Security group on the target does not allow the ALB security group on the health-check port
Target SG inbound rules; NACL on the target subnet allowing ephemeral return ports
Allow the ALB SG as the source on the traffic port; open ephemeral 1024-65535 outbound on the NACL
Uneven traffic across AZs on an NLB
Cross-zone load balancing is OFF by default on NLB and GWLB
Target group attribute load_balancing.cross_zone.enabled
Enable cross-zone load balancing (note the cross-AZ data charge) or keep equal target counts per AZ
Deploys drop in-flight requests
Deregistration delay too short for long requests
Target group attribute deregistration_delay.timeout_seconds (default 300 s)
Raise the delay for long requests, or lower it to speed deploys when requests are short
ELB 5XX high but target 5XX zero
The load balancer itself generated the error, not the app
HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count vs HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count
Treat as an LB/target-availability problem (503/502 path), not an application bug
decision_tables.rule_of_thumb: 503 = nobody home. 502 = they answered badly. 504 = they never answered in time. 460 = the client gave up first.

decision_tables.title: Instances do not appear as Systems Manager managed nodes
rows: Instance missing from Fleet Manager entirely
SSM Agent not installed or not running
Agent status via EC2 Serial Console or user data logs; amazon-ssm-agent service state; AMI vintage
Install/start the agent (preinstalled on Amazon Linux 2/2023, Ubuntu LTS, Windows AMIs); use State Manager to keep it current
Agent running but node still not managed
No instance profile, or profile lacks AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore
IAM role attached to the instance; policy contents
Attach an instance profile with AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore (add CloudWatchAgentServerPolicy if the agent ships metrics/logs)
Private-subnet instances only are missing
No outbound HTTPS 443 path to ssm / ssmmessages / ec2messages
Route table (NAT), SG egress, endpoint presence
Add a NAT gateway route, or create the three interface VPC endpoints with private DNS and an SG allowing 443 from the instance subnets
Session Manager fails to open a session
ssmmessages endpoint blocked or KMS key for session encryption not permitted
SSM preferences (S3/CloudWatch logging, KMS key); session-manager-plugin version
Allow ssmmessages, grant kms:Decrypt/GenerateDataKey on the session key, and update the CLI plugin
Node shows Connection lost
Agent stopped, instance stopped, or credentials expired/role removed
Agent log /var/log/amazon/ssm/amazon-ssm-agent.log; instance state
Restart the agent, reattach the role (role changes require agent restart or reboot)
Run Command targets 0 instances by tag
Tag key/value mismatch or the instances are not managed nodes
Exact tag case; managed-node inventory list
Correct the tag, or fix the managed-node prerequisites first - only managed nodes are targetable
Patch Manager reports non-compliant with no patches applied
Instance not in the patch group, or the maintenance window has no registered target/task
Tag key 'Patch Group'; maintenance window targets and tasks; baseline approval rules
Tag the instance, register the target and the AWS-RunPatchBaseline task in the window
On-premises servers not managed
Not registered as hybrid activations
Activation code/ID and the mi- instance IDs
Create a hybrid activation, install the agent with the activation code, attach a service role
decision_tables.rule_of_thumb: Agent + Role + Network. Every missing-node question is one of those three, checked in that order.

decision_tables.title: CloudFormation stack states and the only correct action
rows: CREATE_FAILED
A resource failed during initial create and rollback is starting or disabled
Events tab sorted oldest-first: the FIRST CREATE_FAILED status reason (quota, AMI not in Region, IAM propagation, name already taken)
Fix the template, permission, or quota named in that first reason; set OnFailure=DO_NOTHING on the retry to keep resources for debugging
ROLLBACK_COMPLETE
Initial create failed and everything was rolled back - the stack is a shell with no usable resources
Nothing to check on the stack itself; read the earlier CREATE_FAILED reason to learn why the create failed
You CANNOT update it and ContinueUpdateRollback does not apply. Delete the stack and create it again
ROLLBACK_FAILED
Rollback of a failed create could not complete
The resource named in the last failure event and whatever still references it (ENI attachment, non-empty bucket, SG in use)
Clear the blocking dependency then delete the stack, using RetainResources for anything that will not delete
UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED
Rollback of a failed update could not complete, usually because a resource was changed outside CloudFormation
The failing resource's live configuration versus the template, and CloudTrail for the out-of-band change that broke it
Fix the resource manually, then call ContinueUpdateRollback - optionally with ResourcesToSkip for resources you will reconcile by hand
UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE_CLEANUP_IN_PROGRESS
Rollback succeeded, old resources are being removed
Nothing - the stack is already usable and the cleanup is cosmetic
Wait - no action needed
DELETE_FAILED
A resource could not be deleted (non-empty S3 bucket, ENI in use, SG referenced, retained resource)
The deletion failure reason on that resource, plus who still holds it (other stacks, Lambda ENIs, other security groups)
Empty/detach the blocking resource, then delete again with RetainResources for anything you must keep
CREATE_IN_PROGRESS for hours on a custom resource or WaitCondition
cfn-signal or the custom-resource Lambda never sent a response to the pre-signed URL
The Lambda's CloudWatch log group for an unhandled exception, and cfn-init/cloud-init logs on the instance for a bootstrap failure
Fix the function to always respond SUCCESS/FAILED, or send the signal manually; a CreationPolicy timeout defaults to PT5M
UPDATE_IN_PROGRESS stuck on an ASG
UpdatePolicy rolling update is waiting for success signals or for instances to become healthy
ASG activity history, target-group health, and whether the new instances are running cfn-signal at all
Fix the bootstrap that never signals; correct MinSuccessfulInstancesPercent, PauseTime, or MaxBatchSize
IMPORT_ROLLBACK_FAILED
Resource import failed and could not roll back
The physical resource identifier supplied against the resource's real properties - imports require an exact match
Fix the identifier or template mismatch and retry the import
REVIEW_IN_PROGRESS
A change set was created but never executed - the stack does not exist yet
The change set list for the stack and what each one would replace
Execute the change set to create the stack, or delete the change set
decision_tables.rule_of_thumb: ROLLBACK_COMPLETE means delete and recreate - there is no other answer. UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED means ContinueUpdateRollback.

decision_tables.title: Auto Scaling group instance churn and scaling failures
rows: Instances launch then terminate in a loop
Health check grace period shorter than boot/bootstrap time
Grace period (300 s from the console, 0 when the group was created by API/CLI/CloudFormation); ASG activity history reason 'failed ELB health checks'
Increase the health check grace period, or speed up bootstrap with a baked AMI / warm pool
ASG never replaces an instance the ALB reports unhealthy
Health check type is EC2, not ELB
ASG health check type setting
Set health check type to ELB so the ASG honours target-group health
Alarm fires but no instances launch
Desired capacity already equals max, or a scaling process is suspended
Max size; suspended processes (Launch, Terminate, AZRebalance)
Raise max size; resume the suspended processes
Instances stuck in Pending:Wait or Terminating:Wait
Lifecycle hook never completed
Lifecycle hook heartbeat timeout (default 3600 s) and the automation that should call CompleteLifecycleAction
Call CompleteLifecycleAction, fix the hook target, or lower the heartbeat timeout
Scaling reacts minutes late
5-minute basic monitoring plus a 300 s cooldown
Detailed monitoring setting; policy type
Enable detailed monitoring (1-minute), switch to target tracking with an instance warm-up, or use predictive/scheduled scaling
Scale-in kills the wrong instances
Default termination policy order (AZ balance, then oldest launch template, then closest to billing hour)
Termination policy; instance protection settings
Set a custom termination policy, enable scale-in protection, or use lifecycle hooks to drain
Capacity spread unevenly across AZs
AZRebalance suspended, or one subnet is out of IP addresses / capacity
Subnet free IPs; suspended AZRebalance; instance type availability per AZ
Free IPs or add subnets, resume AZRebalance, use a mixed instances policy
Launch fails immediately
Bad AMI ID for the Region, missing KMS grant for an encrypted AMI, quota exceeded, or a deleted launch template version
ASG activity history failure message
Fix the AMI/Region, grant the ASG service-linked role kms:CreateGrant on the CMK, raise the quota, pin a valid template version
Spot instances vanish repeatedly
Spot interruptions without capacity rebalancing
Interruption notices; allocation strategy
Enable Capacity Rebalancing, diversify instance types, use price-capacity-optimized
Deployment via new AMI is manual and slow
No instance refresh configured
Launch template versions
Start an instance refresh with MinHealthyPercentage (default 90%) and checkpoints (immutable/rolling deployment)
decision_tables.rule_of_thumb: Churn = grace period or health check type. No scaling = max size or a suspended process. Stuck = a lifecycle hook.

decision_tables.title: VPC connectivity: cannot reach internet / S3 / peer / on-premises
rows: Public-subnet instance has no internet
No IGW route, or no public IP / EIP on the ENI
Route table has 0.0.0.0/0 -> igw; instance public IPv4 address; SG egress
Add the IGW route, assign an EIP or enable auto-assign public IP, allow outbound in the SG
Private-subnet instance has no outbound internet
No NAT route, or the NAT gateway sits in a private subnet
Private route table 0.0.0.0/0 -> nat-; NAT GW subnet must be public with an IGW route and an EIP
Place the NAT GW in a public subnet and point the private route table at it (one per AZ for HA)
Cannot reach S3 from a private subnet with no NAT
Gateway endpoint missing from the subnet's route table
Route table entry with the S3 prefix list -> vpce-; endpoint policy; bucket policy aws:SourceVpce
Associate the gateway endpoint with the correct route tables and relax the endpoint/bucket policy
Interface endpoint name still resolves publicly
Private DNS not enabled, or VPC DNS attributes off
enableDnsSupport and enableDnsHostnames; endpoint Private DNS setting; endpoint SG allows 443
Enable both VPC DNS attributes and Private DNS on the endpoint, allow 443 from the client subnets
Peered VPCs cannot communicate
Route missing on one side, overlapping CIDRs, or SG not allowing the peer CIDR
Both route tables; peering connection status Active; SG rules
Add routes on BOTH sides and allow the peer CIDR/SG; overlapping CIDRs cannot be peered - use PrivateLink
Spoke VPC cannot reach another spoke through the TGW
TGW route table association/propagation missing, or the subnet route to the TGW is absent
TGW attachment association, propagation, and TGW route table entries; subnet route to tgw-
Associate and propagate correctly, and add the subnet route table entry to the TGW
On-premises cannot reach the VPC over VPN
Tunnel down, missing route propagation, or asymmetric routing
Tunnel status, BGP session, route propagation enabled on the route table, customer gateway config
Bring the tunnel up (IKE/PSK/public IP), enable route propagation, allow the on-prem CIDR in SGs/NACLs
Traffic works one way only
NACL missing the ephemeral-port return rule
NACL inbound and outbound rules on both subnets; flow logs showing outbound REJECT
Allow 1024-65535 for return traffic in the appropriate direction
Instance launch fails with insufficient addresses
Subnet exhausted (remember 5 reserved IPs)
Available IP count per subnet; ENIs held by Lambda/EKS/interface endpoints
Add a subnet or a secondary VPC CIDR - subnets cannot be resized
Peer cannot use the other VPC's NAT or IGW
Edge-to-edge routing is not supported over peering
Architecture
Give each VPC its own NAT/IGW, or centralize egress behind a Transit Gateway inspection VPC
decision_tables.rule_of_thumb: Route -> gateway -> public IP -> SG -> NACL -> OS. If it is one-directional, it is a NACL. If it is nothing at all, it is routing.

decision_tables.title: VPC Flow Logs pattern to root cause
rows: Inbound ACCEPT, outbound REJECT for the same flow
A NACL blocked the RETURN traffic (a stateful SG can never do this)
Outbound NACL rules on the source subnet and inbound on the destination subnet, ephemeral range
Allow ephemeral ports 1024-65535 in the NACL direction that is rejecting
Inbound REJECT only
The security group (or an inbound NACL rule) denied the packet on arrival
Destination SG inbound rules for the port/protocol/source; NACL rule order
Add the inbound allow rule to the SG, or fix the lower-numbered deny rule in the NACL
No records at all for the flow
Packets never reached the ENI
Route table, IGW/NAT, upstream firewall, DNS resolving to the wrong IP, or the flow log filter is set to ACCEPT-only
Fix routing/gateway; recreate the flow log with filter ALL
ACCEPT both directions but the app still fails
Network is fine - the problem is above layer 4
Application listening port, OS firewall (iptables/Windows Firewall), TLS/certificate errors, target health checks
Fix the application, OS firewall, or certificate
log-status NODATA
No traffic on that ENI during the aggregation window
Whether the workload was actually running
Nothing to fix - generate traffic or check the right ENI
log-status SKIPDATA
Records were dropped due to internal capacity limits
Volume of traffic; aggregation interval
Not a security issue; reduce noise with filters or accept the gap
Only REJECT records on port 22/3389 from random IPs
Internet background scanning against a public IP
Whether the SG actually allows those ports
Confirm SG denies them; use Session Manager instead of public SSH/RDP
DNS troubleshooting shows nothing in flow logs
Flow Logs do not capture Amazon-provided DNS resolver traffic, IMDS 169.254.169.254, DHCP, or license activation
Route 53 Resolver query logs
Enable Resolver query logging for DNS visibility
decision_tables.rule_of_thumb: Accepted in but rejected out = NACL. Rejected in = security group. Nothing logged = routing.

decision_tables.title: CloudFront caching and delivery problems
rows: Low cache hit ratio
Cache key too specific: forwarding all headers, all cookies, or all query strings
Cache policy contents; x-edge-result-type Miss ratio in logs; CacheHitRate metric
Forward only required values in the cache policy; move the rest to an origin request policy
Low hit ratio despite a tight cache key
Origin sends Cache-Control: no-cache/no-store/private or very short max-age
Origin response headers; MinTTL/DefaultTTL/MaxTTL
Set proper Cache-Control at the origin or raise MinTTL/DefaultTTL in the behaviour
Users still see the old file after a deploy
Objects are cached until TTL expires
TTL settings; whether the file name changed
Invalidate the path (1,000 free paths/month) for a hotfix; use versioned object names as the standing practice
403 Access Denied from an S3 origin
OAC not granted in the bucket policy, or the object is missing while ListBucket is denied (S3 returns 403 not 404)
Bucket policy for the cloudfront.amazonaws.com principal with the distribution ARN condition; object existence; SSE-KMS decrypt permission
Update the bucket policy for OAC, add kms:Decrypt for the CloudFront service principal, and verify the object path
403 from CloudFront for some users only
Geo restriction, WAF rule, or signed URL/cookie expiry
Geo restriction list; WAF web ACL logs; signature expiry
Adjust geo restriction, tune the WAF rule, regenerate signatures
502 from CloudFront
Origin TLS negotiation failure - expired/mismatched certificate or unsupported cipher
Origin protocol policy, origin domain vs certificate CN/SAN, TLS version
Fix or renew the origin certificate and align the minimum TLS/cipher settings
504 from CloudFront
Origin timed out or a firewall/SG blocks the edge
Origin response timeout (default 30 s, keep-alive 5 s), origin SG allowing CloudFront managed prefix list
Raise the origin timeout, speed up the origin, allow the com.amazonaws.global.cloudfront.origin-facing prefix list
Dynamic pages served stale to logged-in users
Personalized content is being cached
Which cookies/headers are in the cache key
Add the session cookie/header to the cache key, or set a cache behaviour with CachingDisabled for that path pattern
Custom domain shows a certificate error
ACM certificate not in us-east-1, or the alternate domain name is missing
Certificate Region; distribution alternate domain names
Issue/import the certificate in us-east-1 and add the CNAME/alias plus alternate domain name
Origin overwhelmed during a spike
No origin shield / no failover, or every request is a miss
Origin Shield setting; origin group configuration
Enable Origin Shield, configure an origin group with failover status codes, raise TTLs
decision_tables.rule_of_thumb: Hit ratio problems are cache-key problems. Stale content is a TTL problem. 403 with S3 is an OAC/bucket-policy problem.

decision_tables.title: RDS and Aurora operational problems
rows: Too many connections / connection errors under bursty load
Connection limit reached (max_connections scales with instance memory); Lambda opening a connection per invocation
DatabaseConnections metric vs max_connections in the parameter group
Put RDS Proxy in front, use application connection pooling, or scale the instance class
Instance in storage-full state
Allocated storage exhausted by data, logs, or temp files
FreeStorageSpace metric; binlog/tempdb growth; whether storage autoscaling is on and what its maximum threshold is

Enable storage autoscaling (it fires only below 10% free, sustained 5 minutes, and 6 hours after the last storage change), increase allocated storage, shorten log retention (storage cannot be shrunk afterwards)
Read replica lag climbing
Write-heavy primary, an undersized replica, long-running transactions, or missing indexes on the replica
ReplicaLag metric; replica instance class; Performance Insights top SQL
